claims.text: FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles begin the solid-to-liquid transition through localized melting in slightly Cu-enriched regions.
Cu-enriched regions melt first because Cu is a lower-melting-point constituent and lowers the effective local melting temperature.
Limited atomic mobility allows local compositional fluctuations to persist during heating.
Localized molten domains generate internal thermal-pressure differences.
Internal thermal-pressure differences cause molten beads to split into smaller droplets.
Molten-bead splitting accelerates coalescence of liquid regions and thereby controls transition progression.
Temperature exposure can govern nanoparticle melting, molten-bead fusion, and molten-bead fission.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are compositionally homogeneous, uniformly solid, and have an even elemental distribution.
Heating will produce early local melting preferentially at Cu-rich locations.
Early local melting will be followed by formation of small molten droplets that merge into a fully molten particle.
Rapid but controlled heating can preserve limited diffusion before complete homogenization or excessive aggregation.
Limited heating time and rapid cooling can prevent excessive nanoparticle growth and agglomeration.
Reducing Cu content should alter the melting-onset temperature or melting progression in a predictable manner.
The Cu-enrichment mechanism is supported by analogous nanoparticle synthesis observations.

contradictions.description: The starting particles are described as compositionally homogeneous with an even elemental distribution, while the proposed initiating mediator requires pre-existing Cu-enriched nanoscopic regions. The hypothesis does not define the allowable fluctuation scale or explain how such enrichment arises under limited mobility.
